sections.sectionSummaryBrief: Joy must be accompanied by awe and humility to prevent it from leading to a sense of self and undesirable consequences.

translations.translation: However, together with this it is written,
"Serve the L-rd with fear,"
except that in this same verse it continues, "and rejoice with trembling,"
which implies that there must be joy.
Rather, when joy is in a felt sense,
it is possible that from this one may come to a feeling of self-existence,
and through this to several undesirable things that branch out from it.
Therefore, it must be "Serve the L-rd with fear and rejoice with trembling,"
so that through this the joy will be
(not in the category of felt sensation,
but rather)
in the category of self-nullification and humility,
and in the language of the verse,
"And the humble shall add joy in the L-rd,"
meaning that the joy is together with or stems from humility and self-nullification
(as will be explained in section 6).

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: The Baal HaYom Huledes explains that Chava and Noach sought joy through sensation, while Sarah alone rectified the sin of the Tree of Knowledge through joy rooted in self-nullification, which brings about true ascent.

translations.translation: And based on this, the Baal HaYom Huledes explains in his aforementioned maamar
the matter of "the wife of Chava... the wife of Sarah...,"
that the common denominator among them is that they wanted to effect the matter of joy.
As our sages said regarding Chava,
"She squeezed a cluster of grapes and gave it to him,"
and regarding Noach it is written,
"And he planted a vineyard and drank of the wine,"
for wine is the matter of joy, as it is written,
"Wine that gladdens G-d and men."
However, with Chava the joy was in the category of felt sensation,
for regarding Chava it is written,
"And the woman saw that the tree was good for food and that it was a desire to the eyes," which is the matter of sensation.
And Noach wanted to rectify the sin of the Tree of Knowledge,
which is the matter of sensation,
through sensation,
and he did not succeed.
For "he drank of the wine" brought him
(not to joy in the category of self-nullification,
"wine that gladdens,"
but rather)
to intoxication,
"wine that intoxicates."
And although in intoxication there is an absence of sensation,
nevertheless, this absence of sensation is not from the aspect of humility and self-nullification, but rather from confusion of the mind
(and sensation).
And the rectification for the sin of the Tree of Knowledge
(the matter of sensation)
was accomplished specifically through Sarah,
[as explained in Kabbalah
that Sarah rectified what Chava corrupted],
for Sarah is the aspect of Malchus
[therefore she is called Sarah, from the term
"dominion"],
the matter of self-nullification,
and therefore specifically through her was the rectification accomplished,
joy that is in the category of self-nullification.
And this is "the wife of Sarah, descending and ascending,"
that from the aspect of self-nullification inherent in Malchus, even when it descends below,
the descent
("descending")
is for the sake of the ascent
("and ascending"),
for the descent of Malchus below is in order to refine and rectify the sparks of holiness found below and to elevate them upward.
And likewise is the descent of
(Avraham and)
Sarah to Egypt
(physically),
which was in order that
the ascent from Egypt,
"And Avram ascended from Egypt, he and his wife,"
would be in a manner of "and Avram was very heavy with cattle, silver, and gold,"
which was accomplished through Sarah, as it is written,
"And He did good to Avram for her sake."
And through this she merited supernal life,
to the extent that "her life was life,"
meaning that the life was hers
(also)
in a felt sense,
for because Malchus is inherently in the category of self-nullification, therefore even its felt aspect is in the category of self-nullification.
And in avodah (divine service) this means,
that even when joy is in revelation, nevertheless it is in the category of self-nullification
[similar to a king who, despite being in loftiness and joy,
"strength and gladness are in His place,"
this is not in the category of self-existence].
And therefore, from this joy,
not only is it not possible that there will be undesirable consequences from it
(as was with Chava and Noach),
but on the contrary, it brings to the ultimate elevation,
even to the level that is analogous to the future to come,
and as explained in the maamar
(of the Baal HaYom Huledes)
that the matter of "her life was life" is analogous to "and we shall live before Him"
that will be in the future,
life in ultimate perfection.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: The joy of the future, "then our mouth will be filled with laughter," is incomparably greater than present joy, and Sarah's son Yitzchak, meaning laughter, alludes to this future joy.

translations.translation: And one may connect this with the verse,
"Then our mouth will be filled with laughter,"
that in the future to come joy will be in ultimate perfection,
to the extent that the joy of the present,
even when it is in ultimate perfection
(as much as is possible now),
is incomparable to the joy and laughter that will be in the future to come,
"Then our mouth will be filled with laughter."
And although the joy of the future to come will come
(like all matters of the future)
through serving G-d with joy during the time of exile,
nevertheless, the reward that will come from this in the future to come
("then our mouth will be filled with laughter")
is beyond measure, even beyond any measure at all,
to the extent that it is above the category of reward.
And based on this, one can explain why the son of Sarah,
for whom Sarah prayed and even more so
(even more than Avraham Avinu),
was named Yitzchak, after "G-d has made laughter for me,"
because the matter of "her life was life"
(of Sarah)
is like "and we shall live before Him" that will be in the future
(as above from the maamar of the Baal HaYom Huledes),
and this is that Sarah's son is Yitzchak, whose meaning is laughter and joy,
even to the laughter and joy that is analogous to "then our mouth will be filled with laughter" of the future to come,
therefore in the future to come they will say to Yitzchak
(specifically)
"for you are our father."
